description: Keeping systems and people safe: cryptography, authentication and authorization, the classic web attacks, network defenses, and the human side of it. Concepts are defensive and explanatory.

concepts.title: Security
concepts.summary: Protecting what matters from people who want it. It's less a wall than an ongoing argument between what a system was meant to allow and what a determined person can make it do.

concepts.title: Cryptography
concepts.summary: The mathematics of secrets and proofs: scrambling messages so only the right person can read them, and showing something is genuine without revealing it. Modern life quietly rests on a few well-tested ideas.

concepts.title: Hashing
concepts.summary: A one-way fingerprint: any input, however large, becomes a short fixed string, and you can't get the input back. Change one bit and the fingerprint changes completely, which makes tampering detectable.

concepts.title: Encryption
concepts.summary: Turning readable data into noise using a key, so that only someone holding the right key can turn it back. The scheme can be public; only the key has to stay secret.

concepts.title: Shared Keys
concepts.summary: One secret key both locks and unlocks. It's fast and strong, but both sides must somehow already share the key, which is exactly the problem public-key methods solve.

concepts.title: Public Keys
concepts.summary: A pair of linked keys: one you publish, one you keep. Anyone can lock a message to you with the public one; only you can open it. It lets strangers set up secrets without ever meeting.

concepts.title: Key Exchange
concepts.summary: Two parties talk in public and end up sharing a secret no eavesdropper can work out. It sounds impossible, and it rests on math that is easy in one direction and very hard to reverse.

concepts.title: Signatures
concepts.summary: Sign with a private key, and anyone can check the result with your public one. It proves who wrote something and that it hasn't changed since, without any ink.

concepts.title: TLS
concepts.summary: The handshake behind the padlock: two machines agree on keys, check each other's identity, then encrypt everything that follows. It protects a connection from being read or altered in transit.

concepts.title: Certificates
concepts.summary: A signed statement that a public key belongs to a named site. Your browser trusts a short list of authorities, who vouch for everyone else, so the whole system rests on that chain of vouching.

concepts.title: HTTPS
concepts.summary: The web's conversation, wrapped in TLS. Nobody along the route can read your requests or quietly change the reply, and the site is who it claims to be.

concepts.title: Authentication
concepts.summary: Proving who you are: something you know, something you have, something you are. Systems combine them, since any one alone can be guessed, stolen, or copied.

concepts.title: Passwords
concepts.summary: The oldest and weakest common secret. People reuse them, guess them, and give them away, so good systems never store the password itself, only something derived from it.

concepts.title: Salting
concepts.summary: Mix random data into each password before hashing it. Two people with the same password then get different stored values, and precomputed lookup tables stop working.

concepts.title: Multi-factor
concepts.summary: Require two different kinds of proof, such as a password and a code from your phone. A thief who has only one still gets nowhere, which blocks most everyday account takeovers.

concepts.title: Sessions
concepts.summary: After you log in, the server hands you a token and you show it with each request, so you don't send your password every time. Protecting that token and expiring it on time are the whole game.

concepts.title: JWT
concepts.summary: A signed, self-contained ticket: who you are and what you may do, readable by anyone and impossible to forge without the signing key. Convenient, and easy to misuse, since revoking one early is hard.

concepts.title: OAuth
concepts.summary: Let one app act on your behalf at another without ever seeing your password. You approve a limited permission, and the app gets a token that can do exactly that and no more.

concepts.title: Biometrics
concepts.summary: Using your body as the password: fingerprints, faces, voices. Convenient, but unlike a password you can't change your face if it leaks, so it works best as one factor among several.

concepts.title: Authorization
concepts.summary: Deciding what someone is allowed to do once you know who they are. Authentication asks who you are; authorization asks what you can touch, and the two are constantly confused.

concepts.title: Roles
concepts.summary: Give permissions to roles like admin or reader, then give people roles. Managing a few dozen roles is far easier than managing thousands of individual permissions.

concepts.title: Least Privilege
concepts.summary: Give every person and program only the access they need, and no more. When something goes wrong, as it will, the damage is limited to what that one thing could reach.

concepts.title: Access Lists
concepts.summary: An explicit list attached to a resource of who may do what to it. Simple and precise, and hard to keep tidy as the list grows.

concepts.title: Web Attacks
concepts.summary: The standard ways sites get broken: tricking them into running someone's script, sending forged requests, or slipping commands into the data. Nearly all come from trusting input a site should have treated as hostile.

concepts.title: XSS
concepts.summary: An attacker gets a page to run their script in your browser by smuggling it into content the site displays. Escaping everything you output, and limiting what scripts may do, closes most of it.

concepts.title: CSRF
concepts.summary: A malicious page makes your browser send a request to a site you're logged into, using your credentials. Tokens that only the real site can produce, and stricter cookies, stop it.

concepts.title: SQL Injection
concepts.summary: Input crafted so a database treats it as a command rather than data. It's prevented by never gluing text into queries, and using parameters that keep data and instructions apart.

concepts.title: Same-Origin Policy
concepts.summary: A browser rule that keeps one site's scripts from reading another's data. It's the wall between your bank tab and everything else, and most web security tools are about controlled gaps in it.

concepts.title: CORS
concepts.summary: How a server tells browsers which other sites may read its responses. It relaxes the same-origin wall deliberately, on the server's terms, rather than leaving developers to bypass it.

concepts.title: CSP
concepts.summary: A header where a site lists where its scripts, images, and frames may come from. Anything else is refused, so even if an attacker injects something, the browser won't run it.

concepts.title: Network Defense
concepts.summary: Controlling what may travel where: filtering traffic, hiding what should be private, and noticing when something looks wrong. Defense in depth means no single layer has to be perfect.

concepts.title: Firewalls
concepts.summary: Rules about which traffic may pass: this port, from that address, in this direction. The default is to refuse, and each opening is a decision someone should be able to explain.

concepts.title: DDoS
concepts.summary: Flooding a service with so much traffic that real users can't get in. Defenses spread the load across many machines and filter out the junk before it arrives.

concepts.title: VPNs
concepts.summary: An encrypted tunnel between you and another network. It protects traffic on an untrusted link, and shifts the question of who you trust from your local network to the VPN's operator.

concepts.title: Intrusion Detection
concepts.summary: Watching traffic and logs for signs of attack, either patterns already known or behavior that looks unusual. It won't stop a breach, but it can shorten how long one goes unnoticed.

concepts.title: Zero Trust
concepts.summary: Assume no request is safe just because it comes from inside. Every user and device must prove itself each time, and get only the access that request needs.

concepts.title: Privacy
concepts.summary: Control over what others know about you and what they do with it. Security is the lock; privacy is deciding who gets a key, and why.

concepts.title: Social Engineering
concepts.summary: Getting past the lock by asking, rather than by breaking it. Urgency, authority, and friendliness are more effective than most exploits, which is why training matters as much as software.

concepts.title: Phishing
concepts.summary: A message pretending to be someone you trust so you'll hand over a password or click a link. The defense is a habit: check who is really asking before you act on it.

concepts.title: Rate Limiting
concepts.summary: Cap how many requests one client can make in a given time. It blunts password guessing, scraping, and floods, and keeps one noisy user from starving everyone else.
